title: Valmiki and the name said backwards
hook: a robber can't bring himself to say Rama's name, so seven sages teach it to him backwards
carry: nama japa: the name works, even said backwards
tomorrow: what came out of Shiva's drum?

segments.voice: Yesterday, vibhuti: Krishna shining in the best of everything, even the letter a. Today, a name built on that sound, and a robber who learned it backwards.

Before he wrote the Ramayana, Valmiki was a robber. That's how he tells it himself, in a later Sanskrit retelling called the Adhyatma Ramayana. He lived among hunters and robbed travelers on the forest road. One day seven sages came down that road, and he raised his weapon. The sages didn't run. They asked him one question. Your family eats what you steal. Will they share the weight of what you've done? Go and ask them.
screen: `A ROBBER ON THE FOREST ROAD.` → `SEVEN SAGES.` → `WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE IT?`

segments.voice: He went home and asked. Every one of them said no: that's yours. He came back shaken and fell at the sages' feet. They gave him the name of Rama to repeat, but in the telling they gave it to him backwards: mara. The way the story is usually explained, he was too far gone even to say it straight. Say mara, mara, mara, over and over, and listen. It turns into Rama, Rama. He sat and repeated it so long that an anthill, a valmika, rose up over his body. When the sages came back and called him out of it, he had a new name, for the anthill: Valmiki. Here's the teaching. It's called nama japa, repeating the name of God, and many Hindus hold it as the simplest practice there is, and one of the strongest. The robber didn't have to be good first. He didn't even have to say it right. The name did its work anyway. That's why some devotees fill whole notebooks writing Shri Rama, a practice called likhita japa, written japa, and why the name is said at the start of a journey and at the end of a life. Now listen to the name itself. Written carefully, Rāma has a small line over the first a. That line marks length, matra, the measure of a sound in time. A short vowel takes one measure; a long one about two. Rāma is long, then short: Raah-muh. Chanted again and again, that long ā is where the voice rests.
screen: `EVERY ONE OF THEM SAID NO.` · `MARA, MARA: IT TURNS INTO RAMA.` · `NAMA JAPA: REPEATING THE NAME.` · `THE NAME DID ITS WORK.` · then, large: `RĀMA: LONG, THEN SHORT.`

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say a short a, quick and soft, then a long ā, held about twice as long. Then begin the name slowly, Rāma, long then short. Or begin the robber's way, mara, mara, and let it turn. If you pray, let this be a small japa, a few rounds; if not, just listen to the measure of the sound.
Matra. The length of a sound in time: the line over the first a in Rāma, where the voice stays longer.
Your line: nama japa, the name works, even said backwards. Tomorrow: what came out of Shiva's drum? See you then.

screen: `DAY 1041 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT CAME OUT OF SHIVA'S DRUM?`

howItsDone: Many Hindus practice nama japa, repeating a name of God aloud, silently, or in writing (likhita japa, filling notebooks with 'Shri Rama'); the story of Valmiki the robber, changed by repeating the name, is told to show that anyone may begin. Reciters also keep the long and short vowels of the name, as in Rāma.

fork.reveal: the sages gave a robber the name backwards, mara, and he rose as Valmiki. nama japa doesn't wait for you to be good first.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: ā, the long partner of a. In transliteration it gets a line on top.

chat.meaning: Nama japa, repeating God's name, can be said or written. The robber who became Valmiki was changed by repeating Rama's name, even backwards.

Valmiki.meaning: the poet of the Ramayana; once a robber, in the Adhyatma telling

Adhyatma Ramayana.meaning: a later Sanskrit retelling of Rama's story

japa.meaning: repeating a name of God or a mantra

Rāma.meaning: the prince of Ayodhya, hero of the Ramayana

matra.meaning: length: the measure of a sound in time

recall: a joining, where night meets day

notes: Editor pass: cut the unsupported 'most of the time' from the hook; replaced the garbled 'the people who carry them' with 'anyone who hears them'.
Day 2 of 7 in 'Sanskrit sounds for readers'.
'A short vowel takes one matra, a long about two' is stated as the tradition of recitation ('the tradition measures'), not from the cited text. Confirm wording.

Pronunciation guides (Rah-muh, See-tah, Kur-muh, Shi-vuh) are rough English approximations; final short a as 'uh' is standard in modern recitation. Confirm Śiva is short i, short a, and that Gītā has two long vowels.
'Sanskrit verse is built out of patterns of short and long syllables' is a general claim about meter, not from the cited text; a Keeper may prefer 'tradition says'.
Respect line: 'nothing is wrong with how English speakers say these names' is meant to avoid shaming anglicized pronunciations; confirm tone.

Audit pass: meter line corrected; classical meter counts light and heavy syllables (laghu/guru), where a short vowel before two consonants also counts heavy, so "built out of short and long syllables" was loose.
